Lessons.Title: Use a Protractor to Measure Angles
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 Grade 4 Unit 7 Lesson 9: use a real protractor to measure angles in 1° increments, and identify 1° as 1/360 of a complete turn. This lesson follows previous clock and benchmark estimates: one degree is a finer unit of angular measurement.

2021 lesson activities: Warm-up: True or False: There's Something about 45 (10 minutes); Activity 1: How Large is a $1^\circ$ Angle? (15 minutes); Activity 2: Use a Protractor (20 minutes); Cool-down: Measure the Angles (5 minutes)

Corrected mathematical focus: position protractor centre on vertex, align its baseline with the first ray, and read the scale beginning at zero on THAT ray. A second scale often displays a complementary measure, so determine whether the angle is acute or obtuse before selecting a reading.

2021 local source warm-up has FOUR equations: 2×45=6×15 (true: 90=90), 4×45=2×90 (true: 180=180), 3×45=180−90 (false: 135≠90), and 6×45=45+90+135 (true: 270=270). Explain structure and multiplication, not just true/false.

Activity 1 asks what fractions of a full turn 120°, 60°, 45°, 30°, 10°, and 1° represent; students inspect one-degree tick increments on a real protractor and measure pictured angles using unnumbered protractor marks, with teacher review. Independent digital fraction benchmarks are supplementary, not claimed as original publisher figures.

Activity 2 shows FOUR original printed angle/protractor pairs and asks pupils to measure each. Elena reports 80° and Kiran 100° for an original angle. Original teacher synthesis says the angle is visibly greater than 90°; therefore Kiran's 100° reading, not Elena's 80°, matches the source explanation. Teacher still checks the original drawing, ray placement, work and rationale.

First-party Edulytics Cool-down (NOT original publisher Measure the Angles): draw a 65° angle using a physical protractor; explain the choice of zero scale and measure again. Teacher checks construction. Supplementary exact digital practice provides text-based paired scale labels, and grades only the correct zero-aligned degree reading, not the actual construction or original diagrams.

KeyConcepts.Title: Degree is a fraction of a turn
KeyConcepts.Definition: A complete 360° turn contains 360 equal one-degree turns.
KeyConcepts.Rule: An angle of n° is n/360 of a complete revolution; reduce if asked.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measure an angle with a protractor
KeyConcepts.Definition: Protractors display calibrated ticks and frequently opposing printed number scales.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Centre on the vertex, put one ray on the zero baseline, then follow the scale that begins at zero there.
KeyConcepts.Example: A described second ray showing outer 80° and inner 100° is measured 100° if the initial ray aligns with INNER zero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Source figure and student reasoning
KeyConcepts.Definition: The 2021 teacher lesson uses four printed angles and one 80°/100° disagreement.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For the original obtuse example Kiran's 100° is supported by the source teacher synthesis; actual original diagrams and construction must be seen and reviewed by teacher.
KeyConcepts.Example: An angle greater than 90° cannot measure 80°.

WorkedExamples.Title: All four 2021 source warm-up equalities
WorkedExamples.Question: For each, say true or false and explain: 2×45=6×15; 4×45=2×90; 3×45=180−90; 6×45=45+90+135.
WorkedExamples.Method: Evaluate both sides and use angle benchmark multiples of 45.

WorkedExamples.Title: 2021 source Activity 1: degrees as parts of a turn
WorkedExamples.Question: What fraction of a 360° turn do 120°, 60°, 45°, 30°, 10° and 1° represent?
WorkedExamples.Method: For n degrees, write n/360 and simplify.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every degree fraction is n divided by 360.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source: 80° versus 100°
WorkedExamples.Question: Elena says 80° and Kiran says 100° for the protractor-overlay angle. Which conclusion is supported?
WorkedExamples.Method: Estimate acute vs obtuse before following the scale that begins at zero on the first ray.
Steps: The source teacher synthesis states that the pictured angle is greater than a 90° right angle.
80° is acute and is therefore ruled out.
100° is obtuse; the source teacher explanation supports Kiran's reading.
The precise original drawing still requires teacher viewing to assess student measuring skill.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 100° (Kiran) according to the original 2021 teacher synthesis.

WorkedExamples.Title: Digital-only independent two-scale reading
WorkedExamples.Question: Text-only protractor: the first ray aligns with INNER zero, and the second ray crosses outer 80° / inner 100°. What is the angle?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read from the zero-aligned INNER scale to the crossing of the other ray.
Steps: Determine which zero the initial ray touches: inner zero.
Choose the inner reading on the second ray: 100°.
The outer 80° is the opposite scale's complementary reading.
WorkedExamples.Check: 80°+100°=180°; only one scale starts at zero on the first ray.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original four physical protractor angles (teacher-scored)
WorkedExamples.Question: Use the four lawfully available source figures to measure the printed angles.
WorkedExamples.Method: Centre the transparent protractor at each vertex and place its baseline along a source ray.
Steps: Estimate whether the angle is acute/obtuse before measuring.
Read the correct scale from the aligned zero to the second ray.
Write the result in degrees and justify measurement to teacher.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Depends on each original printed figure; no made-up numerical labels.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source figures/physical positioning cannot be certified by text-only generator.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent Edulytics Cool-down (teacher-scored)
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw and measure an angle of exactly 65° with your protractor.
WorkedExamples.Method: Position protractor centre on vertex, one ray on zero, mark 65° on that scale and draw the second ray.
Steps: Draw and label vertex P and first ray.
Align centre and baseline; use the correct 65° tick.
Draw second ray, remeasure, show teacher.
WorkedExamples.Check: First-party equivalent, NOT the publisher's gated assessment.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choosing 80° from the wrong scale on the source obtuse angle.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original teacher synthesis explicitly identifies the picture as greater than 90°.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Estimate acute versus obtuse first, then choose the scale beginning at aligned zero; Kiran's 100° is supported.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reading the other protractor scale or measuring from the wrong zero.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The printed numbers are opposite, and a second ray can appear at two different labels.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Follow only the number sequence beginning at zero where the INITIAL ray lies.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting unnumbered 1° marks as if each mark represents 10° or treating a digital verbal prompt as physically measuring.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Each small tick can be one degree, and physical alignment matters.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count one-degree increments, inspect the physical original figure, and have teacher confirm work.

SummaryPoints: 1° is exactly 1/360 of one complete 360° rotation; the original six turn fractions should be simplified.
Source warm-up: true, true, false, true across all FOUR equations.
Source Elena (80°) versus Kiran (100°): original teacher guidance identifies the angle as obtuse, so Kiran's 100° is correct.
Align protractor centre and initial ray, then follow the appropriate zero scale.
Original four source figures and any physical construction are teacher-reviewed; digital exact texts are supplemental.
Edulytics first-party 65° construction Cool-down substitutes for unavailable publisher assessment.
